correctness.rationale: Averaging all-zero-window incidences across all nonzero affine functions gives the sharp universal bound for 1≤b≤m. Primitive-field trace functionals have exact cyclic b-tuple counts; insertion of the zero field coordinate changes a run count by at most one, matching the bound simultaneously. The primitive polynomial p(1)=1 forbids m+1 consecutive ones in a trace m-sequence and insertion arguments forbid m+1 consecutive zeros in any nonzero affine word, giving full length from b=m+1. All boundary widths and nonzero-codeword restrictions were reconstructed. A separate direct evaluator checks all m=2..8 and all rooted permutations at m=3; finite evidence is corroboration only.

originality.rationale: The new quantification is a maximum over every coordinate permutation and all window widths simultaneously. The closest published fixed-order Reed–Muller theorem is not stronger: at m=4,b=3 its value is 10 versus the realized sharp optimized value 14. The cyclic simplex results omit the zero evaluation coordinate and affine constant. General b-symbol bounds, related pair cases and accessible records do not imply the full hierarchy. Historical priority remains qualified, not asserted unique.
residual_risks: An unindexed earlier Reed–Muller/Hadamard code permutation optimization or m-sequence interpretation could imply the formula; current searches and inspected closest primary theorems found no such domination.

The numerical coincidence with generalized Hamming weights warrants historical specialist comparison; a weight-hierarchy identity alone does not prove the existence of this simultaneous circular ordering.
Historical priority is a literature judgment without independent audit, not a guarantee of first discovery.

value.rationale: The problem optimizes a natural overlapping-read decoding metric on a standard evaluation code over all coordinate layouts, a parameter not fixed by Hamming equivalence. The theorem gives a sharp complete hierarchy and one simultaneous optimizer in all dimensions, with a universal obstruction and explicit trace-sequence construction. At fixed b≥2 the gain over the standard lexicographic layout scales with the code length. It is not dependent on tiny finite improvements or code replay; it makes no unsupported downstream performance assertions.
